[SQLite backup semantics](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_vacuum.html) and
[WAL file handling](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html#the_wal_file) describe the storage
rules behind these procedures.


<!-- ===== mqlite main · source v0.4.1; latest supported release v0.4.0 · docs/turso.md ===== -->

# Turso / libSQL: concurrency & embedded replicas (MQLITE-4)

MQLite runs the same engine on a local SQLite file or a remote
[Turso](https://turso.tech)/libSQL database — set `MQLITE_DB=libsql://<db>.turso.io`
(+ `MQLITE_DB_AUTH_TOKEN`). The remote path is **CGO-free**: it speaks Hrana over
HTTP via `libsql-client-go`, so the single static binary still has no native deps.
This note records how concurrency is handled and why embedded replicas are *not*
used.

## Backend parity contract

Storage selection is a deployment detail, not a second API mode. Given the same
committed state, broker time and request, local SQLite and remote Turso/libSQL
MUST produce the same successful result, validation outcome, message/resource
state transition and logical sentinel error. The HTTP status/code mapping and Go
SDK `errors.Is` behavior therefore do not change when an operator changes the
broker's database DSN. In particular, scheduling, delivery counts, settlement,
ordering, deduplication, topic fan-out, deletion and TTL use one engine contract.

This is parity of deterministic queue behavior, not a claim that a local file and
a network service have identical failure or performance envelopes. The documented
differences are operational or failure-boundary concerns:

- latency, throughput and temporary availability caused by the remote round trip;
- remote transport/storage failures, including `ErrOutcomeUnknown` when a write
  may have committed but its acknowledgement was lost;
- retry and cancellation mechanics during a storage fault — notably, a remote
  transactional-outbox callback may run more than once and must keep its effects
  transaction-bound;
- deployment and maintenance controls: the local file lock, SQLite synchronous
  mode, file-size accounting and compaction have no identical remote operation;
  Turso still requires one logical MQLite owner but cannot use that local OS lock;
  and
- explicitly operational observation fields such as backend identity and
  connection-pool data.

Those differences MUST NOT silently change a successful operation's queue
semantics or turn a documented logical error into a backend-specific one. The
hermetic suite locks the shared engine and error mappings on every PR; the
credentials-gated nightly suite compares representative lifecycle, concurrency,
settlement, access-key and TTL contracts with a real Turso database.

## Concurrency model

MQLite has a **single logical owner** in both modes: each database has exactly one
active MQLite broker or embedded `Engine`. Replace that owner stop-then-start after
confirming the old process has exited. Do not use rolling overlap against the same
database. What differs between storage modes is the connection pool:

| | local file / `:memory:` | `libsql://` (HTTP Hrana) | `ws://` / `wss://` |
|---|---|---|---|
| write ownership | 1 connection = local writer (file lock, MQLITE-6) | one broker owns a 4-connection pool; Turso serializes commits | same remote ownership |
| writer pool | MaxOpen=1, MaxIdle=1 | MaxOpen=4, MaxIdle=0 | MaxOpen=4, MaxIdle=2 |
| observation | file: 1 read-only connection; `:memory:`: writer connection | provider-backed pool | provider-backed pool |
| lifecycle | ConnMaxLifetime=0 | one logical Hrana connection per `database/sql` lease | IdleTime=3s, Lifetime=55s |
| physical reuse | SQLite connection stays open | `http.DefaultTransport` still reuses TCP/TLS connections | the WebSocket itself is pooled |

A small remote pool is safe within that one MQLite process because the Turso
primary serializes writes across its connections; this does not make two brokers
or embedded `Engine` instances safe. On `libsql://`, a lease is one ordinary
operation or one complete transaction. Returning the lease discards its logical
Hrana connection before it can enter an idle slot or be handed directly to a
waiting caller; this does **not** tear down the shared HTTP transport or its
TCP/TLS keep-alive connections. Each broker process shares its expensive all-queue
observation query for about 10 seconds on both local and remote backends; separate
brokers do not share that cache. Per-queue `Stats` and each observation's
lightweight storage probe still use the backend shown above.

## Connection resilience (the remote hardening)

An HTTP Hrana response can succeed with a null baton, which means the server has
closed that logical stream. The pinned `libsql-client-go` records the closed state
but does not implement `driver.Validator`. Without the MQLite adapter,
`database/sql` can therefore put a known-closed connection in an idle slot or hand
it directly to a waiting caller; the next operation then fails locally with a
wrapped `driver.ErrBadConn` (`"stream is closed: driver: bad connection"`) before
making an HTTP request. An explicit `*sql.Conn` also cannot exchange its pinned
driver connection underneath the caller.

MQLite prevents that stale handoff for `libsql://`: its compatibility adapter
marks every logical connection invalid when the `database/sql` lease ends. A
transaction remains one uninterrupted lease through commit or rollback. This is
a connection-validity rule, not broader retry, caching or singleflight; physical
HTTP/TLS reuse remains owned by Go's shared transport. Normal failure handling is
still bounded as follows:

- **Bounded retry on transient errors only** — `maxConnAttempts = 6`.
- **Reads retry on any transport drop.** `retryable = remote && (isConnErr || isBusyErr)`
  gates `query`/`queryRowScan`: a read is idempotent, so replaying it on a fresh pooled
  connection is always safe. `isConnErr` spans the whole transport-failure family —
  `driver.ErrBadConn`, a closed Hrana stream, and their siblings `EOF` / `broken pipe` /
  `i/o timeout` (behind a proxy like Fly a dropped connection reads as `EOF`, not `RST`).
- **Writes retry only when the statement provably never applied** — `retryableWrite =
  remote && (ErrBadConn || isBusyErr)`. A closed stream (`ErrBadConn`) or a `SQLITE_BUSY`
  (lock never acquired) guarantees the write never ran, so replaying `exec` / the `inTx`
  commit cannot double-apply. The retry is bounded by `maxConnAttempts`; exhaustion is
  returned to the caller. The `busy_timeout(5000)` DSN pragma belongs to local modernc
  SQLite connections and does not apply to Turso/libSQL.
- **A lost write acknowledgement is _outcome-unknown_, not retried** (MQLITE-59). Any
  other transport drop on a write/commit — the primary may have durably committed before
  the ack was lost — surfaces as `ErrOutcomeUnknown` (HTTP `503 outcome_unknown`) instead
  of being blindly replayed into a double-insert. The caller reconciles by
  `message_id`/dedup before retrying; transparent recovery would need durable per-op
  idempotency, which is deferred. **`errors.Is(err, mqlite.ErrOutcomeUnknown)` works in
  both embedded and client mode.**
- **Never retry a logical storage error.** A constraint violation or `no such table`
  is final inside the engine. At the HTTP client boundary, lifecycle deletion is
  more conservative: every HTTP 5xx is `ErrOutcomeUnknown`, because a gateway can
  synthesize that response after the broker committed and its acknowledgement was
  lost. Local stores never retry at all (a single conn is the single writer).

> **Transport caveat.** The outcome-unknown guarantee holds for the documented remote
> transport `libsql://` (Hrana-over-HTTP). The `ws://`/`wss://` transports can wrap a
> response-read failure as `ErrBadConn`, under which a lost commit ack *would* be
> replayed — prefer `libsql://` for at-least-once remote writes.

The null-baton, idle-pool, direct-waiter, authentication and transaction-lease
contracts are tested hermetically by
`TestHranaClosedStreamIsDiscardedBeforeFreshReuse` and
`TestHranaTransactionKeepsOneLease`. The classifier is pinned by
`TestIsConnErr` / `TestRetryableWrite` / `TestRetryableAndAttempts` in
`engine/storage_test.go`, and broker→SDK propagation by `TestFailOutcomeUnknown`
(server) + `TestRemoteOutcomeUnknownPropagates` (root), so the retry contract can't
silently drift without credentials.

Ordinary and AttemptID `Receive` transactions issue their fenced
`UPDATE messages ... RETURNING` before reading queue or receive-attempt metadata.
This avoids upgrading a deferred read snapshot after another pooled connection has
committed a write. The first update also verifies the queue lifecycle, absolute
subscription expiry and claim-relevant cached configuration. If it returns no row,
the same write transaction reads current metadata to distinguish an empty queue,
deletion/expiry, stale configuration and an AttemptID replay. Batch continuation
then uses the smaller indexed claim statement.

This write-first shape addresses claim transactions in one broker or embedded
`Engine`. Remote retries remain bounded, other operations may still surface
`SQLITE_BUSY`, and the change does not make overlapping brokers against one database
safe.

## Embedded replicas — evaluated, not adopted

Turso embedded replicas keep a **local libSQL file that syncs from the remote
primary**: reads hit the local copy, writes go to the primary and sync back. They
are a big win for read-heavy, geo-distributed *read* workloads. They are the wrong
fit for MQLite, for two independent reasons:

1. **Async sync breaks queue consistency.** A queue's reads (`claim`, `peek`) run
   against the *same* rows it just wrote and need read-after-write consistency: a
   claim must see its own state change atomically. A replica that lags the primary
   by even a sync interval could re-hand-out an already-claimed message or hide a
   just-enqueued one — exactly the correctness the Peek-Lock model exists to
   prevent. The broker is the single logical owner, so it gains nothing from a read
   replica of its own writes.
2. **They require CGO.** Embedded replicas live in the native `go-libsql` binding,
   not the pure-Go `libsql-client-go` Hrana client MQLite uses. Adopting them would
   reintroduce CGO and cross-compilation pain — abandoning the CGO-free,
   single-static-binary goal that defines this project.

**For HA / geo-distribution:** co-locate the broker next to its Turso primary
(low-latency Hrana), or run independent broker + DB pairs per region. Revisit this
decision only when a maintained pure-Go driver satisfies synchronous
read-your-writes semantics, the Go 1.21 floor and every supported release target.

## Validation status

```
hermetic (always, in CI)   engine/storage_test.go    conn-error retry classifier
live  (creds-gated, nightly) engine/turso_test.go     full lifecycle vs real Turso
```

Run the live suite only against a dedicated, disposable test database. `TestMain`
drops every MQLite-managed table before the selected tests begin, including when
`-run` selects one test, so the reset requires an explicit confirmation:

```sh
MQLITE_TEST_DB=libsql://<db>.turso.io MQLITE_TEST_DB_AUTH_TOKEN=<jwt> \
  MQLITE_TEST_DB_RESET_CONFIRM=1 \
  go test ./engine -run TestTurso -v
```

Without `MQLITE_TEST_DB` the live tests skip; the hermetic classifier test always
runs.


<!-- ===== mqlite main · source v0.4.1; latest supported release v0.4.0 · docs/retention.md ===== -->

# Retention, deletion, and storage reclamation

This page follows current `main`, which reports v0.4.1 as an unreleased candidate.
The latest supported release is v0.4.0; use that tag's documentation for deployed
v0.4.0 brokers. v0.3.3 is withdrawn and unsupported; its public artifacts remain
available for forensic or compatibility inspection and must not be deployed. The
v0.4.1 candidate retains v0.4.0's retraction of v0.3.3. v0.3.2 has DLQ retention
and automatic local reclamation, but the work budgets below describe current
`main` unless a version difference is stated.
v0.3.2 does not have the
queue and subscription lifecycle APIs introduced in v0.4.0.

## What removes retained messages

Default Peek-Lock delivery is at-least-once. Receive-and-delete is the explicit
at-most-once broker-removal alternative and removes a message before returning it;
retrying the same receive attempt ID can replay its saved response. A durable
message stays retained until a documented lifecycle action removes or moves it:

| Stored state | Normal lifecycle | Other authorized removal |
|---|---|---|
| `active` | Receive, then Complete or receive-and-delete | message TTL with discard; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry |
| `locked` | Complete, or lock expiry returns it to `active` / moves it to the DLQ at the delivery limit | message TTL with discard; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry |
| `deferred` | ReceiveDeferred, then settle | message TTL with discard; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry |
| `scheduled` | activation at its due time; Cancel only for a scheduled send that has never been delivered | message TTL with discard; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry |
| `dead_lettered` | Redrive or Purge | configured DLQ retention; forced queue/subscription deletion; subscription expiry |

Complete and receive-and-delete remove the row immediately. A message TTL either
moves an expired message to the DLQ or discards it according to
`dead_letter_on_expire`. The queue default is also a ceiling for an explicit Send
TTL. Its clock starts at the message's initial visibility time, so scheduled waiting
does not consume it; later delayed Abandon does not restart it. Expired locks are
reclaimed by the reaper and can be delivered again, so consumers must be idempotent.

Deduplication rows, settlement receipts, and receive-attempt records have their
own expiry-based background cleanup. They are operational replay metadata, not a
message archive; those expiry deletes are not row-budgeted per pass.

## DLQ retention

`mqlite serve` applies default retention targets to dead letters. Every 60 seconds
the retention worker deletes the oldest matching dead letters in bounded batches.
These are asynchronous cleanup targets, not admission limits: a queue can
temporarily exceed its age, count, or byte target between passes or while cleanup
catches up. The worker never deletes active, locked, deferred, or scheduled rows.

| Setting | Broker default | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| `MQLITE_DLQ_MAX_AGE` | `336h` (14 days) | delete dead letters older than this, measured from original enqueue time |
| `MQLITE_DLQ_MAX_COUNT` | `1000000` per queue | keep at most this many dead letters |
| `MQLITE_DLQ_MAX_BYTES` | `0` | optional per-queue cap on dead-letter body bytes; zero disables this bound |
| `MQLITE_DLQ_RETENTION` | enabled | set to `off` to disable all broker defaults |

Embedded engines leave engine-wide DLQ retention defaults disabled unless the
application passes `WithDLQRetention(maxAge, maxCount, maxBytes)`. A positive
per-queue bound still enables that dimension for its queue.

Each queue can override the engine or broker defaults through `QueueConfig`, the
wire `config` object, or `mqlite create-queue`:

| Per-queue value | Effective behavior |
|---:|---|
| `0` | inherit the engine or broker default |
| positive | use this queue-specific bound |
| negative | explicitly leave that dimension unbounded |

The fields are `dlq_max_age_ms`, `dlq_max_count`, and `dlq_max_bytes`. Age uses
`enqueued_at`, not the time at which the message entered the DLQ. Count and byte
limits drop the oldest dead letters first.

Monitor DLQ count, age, and storage size even when defaults are enabled. A growing
active backlog is a consumer-capacity problem and is deliberately outside the DLQ
retention policy.

## Queue and subscription retirement

On `main`, queue and subscription deletion is empty-only by default. `force=true`
is durable authorization to discard all retained states, including locked work,
plus resource-owned deduplication and replay metadata. A locked delivery may
already have caused an external effect; deleting its row cannot undo that effect.

A fixed subscription TTL grants the same discard authorization in advance. Its
absolute deadline is saved on first creation and does not move when the filter is
updated, a message is published or received, or creation is retried. At the
deadline the subscription immediately leaves topic fan-out and its data plane.
Physical cleanup follows in the background. Explicit deletion remains the normal
completion path; TTL is a forgotten-cleanup backstop.

The accepting transaction changes the resource to `deleting` and starts bounded
cleanup. If that cleanup finishes, the same commit removes the resource and the
call returns `deleted`; otherwise the committed `deleting` marker reserves the
name while restart-safe cleanup removes its rows. The foreground request removes
at most 1,000 rows and targets about 8 MiB. Each continuation pass removes
at most 4,096 physical rows and targets about 8 MiB. Its ordinary per-resource
path visits at most 32 local resources, or one such resource on remote Turso/libSQL.
A separate set-based path can finalize up to 512 empty subscriptions
without consuming that 32-or-1 resource-count allowance; their mapping and backing
queue rows still consume the shared row budget. One oversized row may exceed the
byte target so cleanup can still make progress.

The default subscription capacity is 10,000 active plus deleting mappings. A
mapping continues to occupy a slot until physical cleanup finishes. Large forced
deletes or simultaneous expiry waves can therefore create cleanup backlog, grow
the WAL, delay name reuse, and temporarily reject new subscription creation.

For routine request/reply traffic, keep a stable reply subscription and dispatch
with `correlation_id`. If a temporary subscription is necessary, use a globally
unique one-use name, delete it explicitly when finished, add a fixed TTL as a
backstop, and stagger deadlines. Drain before deletion when practical. Reserve
force for intentional abandonment.

One controller must serialize deletion and same-name recreation. After an
uncertain response, use the read-only paged inventory with deleting entries
included. Wait until the name is absent before recreating it, and do not replay an
old delete after a replacement exists.

## Local file reclamation

Deleting a row makes SQLite pages reusable immediately; it does not promise that
the database or WAL file will shrink at once. New local databases use
`auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL`.

On `main`, the background reclaimer runs every 60 seconds. Once at least 256 pages
are free, it checkpoints and returns at most 256 pages per pass to the operating
system. One-off large deletions can therefore need several passes. v0.3.2 uses the
same interval and threshold but attempts to drain the current freelist in one pass;
it does not have `main`'s 256-page work cap. WAL size can also grow while a reader
holds a snapshot, then shrink after checkpointing when that reader finishes.

Operator commands provide explicit reclamation:

- `mqlite vacuum` checkpoints and exhausts the current incremental-vacuum
  freelist. It is the normal manual choice after a large purge.
- `mqlite vacuum --full` rewrites the database and holds the global writer. Use it
  only in a deliberate maintenance window.

Remote Turso/libSQL manages its physical storage. The client does not expose its
database or WAL file size, and local vacuum commands do not apply.

Size local storage for the peak simultaneous backlog, WAL growth, backup space,
and the time needed for bounded cleanup and reclamation. Alert on free disk,
retained/deleting inventory, maintenance failures, and oldest message age rather
than assuming file size will fall immediately after a delete.

## Exporting dead letters before deletion

MQLite has no built-in archive sink. An operator can use existing operations:

1. Quiesce or otherwise coordinate changes to the selected DLQ range.
2. Read dead letters with `Peek(state=dead_lettered)`, advancing `from` past the
   last exported sequence number, and durably write them to external storage.
3. Verify the external copy.
4. After quiescing, purge only after the export covers the intended DLQ. Use
   `max` or `older_than` bounds where appropriate. Alternatively, Redrive to a
   queue whose consumer writes each message to the archive before completing it.

Peek is non-destructive and does not make the export and purge one transaction.
Redrive moves each selected internal batch atomically: source deletion and target
insertion commit together. Delivery from the dedicated queue to an external
archive remains at-least-once, so the archive consumer must be idempotent; Redrive
does not make the external archival handoff one transaction.


<!-- ===== mqlite main · source v0.4.1; latest supported release v0.4.0 · docs/benchmark.md ===== -->

# mqlite benchmarks, sizing & tuning

Measured, reproducible numbers for the mqlite engine across realistic workloads —
**not** a single throughput figure — plus what they mean for **deployment sizing** and
**tuning**. The suite exercises throughput, write amplification, **whole-process memory
+ reclamation**, **DB-file bloat vs reclamation**, **KV-property (enriched) messages**, a
**body-size sweep**, and **load ramp / consumer churn**. Run **locally** (a fast
multi-core box) and on a deliberately tiny **cloud** box so the two tell different truths.

> Philosophy: measure before claiming. Each result below names its harness and
> environment; committed harnesses include `test/bench/` and native Go benchmarks.
> These are historical workload measurements, not capacity guarantees for any release.
> Recheck the current binary
> with your message sizes, concurrency, queue count and monitoring load before
> selecting a memory or CPU limit.

## Sizing & deployment (Fly.io)

The historical sample below ran a single broker on a 256 MB Fly machine. Treat
these measurements as starting points for a workload-specific sizing test; they
do not establish a safe backlog threshold or the current release image size.

```
┌─────────────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ resource    │ measured (1 broker)      │ Fly choice                            │
├─────────────┼──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ memory      │ 19 MB idle               │ 256 MB used in the historical test   │
│             │ 38 MB @ 50k msgs queued  │ validate current peak memory first   │
│             │                          │ no universal backlog threshold        │
│ disk        │ ~0.4 KB / 256 B message  │ 1 GB volume  (~1.1M planned msgs)     │
│             │ + ~4 MB WAL in this run  │   size = backlog × 0.6 KB × 1.5       │
│ vCPU        │ tiny/op; 1000s/s batched │ 1 shared vCPU in the measured setup   │
│ image       │ 10.9 MiB static binary   │ distroless/scratch ≈ 15 MB image,     │
│             │   (CGO-free)             │   cold start < 1 s (scale-to-zero ok) │
└─────────────┴──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Topology:** mqlite is **single-writer**: run one broker or embedded `Engine` per
database. A local process holds a file lock, so run one machine per volume and do
not horizontally scale several machines onto the same SQLite file. Turso/libSQL
provides managed remote storage, but it does not make overlapping brokers safe; see
[turso.md](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/turso.md).

Peak backlog depth is a primary disk-sizing input, rather than lifetime throughput
(`Complete`/`Purge` delete rows). Also budget for WAL growth, SQLite page and index
overhead, reclamation lag, readers that delay checkpoints, and backups. Background
`incremental_vacuum` returns freed pages to the OS over time (see §3), but does not
make the backlog estimate a hard file-size ceiling:

| backlog depth (256 B msgs) | DB on disk | Fly volume |
|--------------:|-----------:|:-----------|
| 100k          | ~40 MB     | 1 GB       |
| 1M            | ~0.4 GB    | 1 GB       |
| 5M            | ~2 GB      | 3 GB       |

## Environments

| | Local (baseline) | Cloud (constrained) |
|---|---|---|
| Where | Docker (`run-bench.sh`) on the dev machine | Fly.io app `mqlite-bench`, region `sin` |
| CPU | 12 vCPU, arm64 (Apple Silicon, linuxkit VM) | **shared-cpu-1x → `GOMAXPROCS=1`** (a *fraction* of one amd64 core, CPU-steal) |
| Memory | 8 GB | **256 MB** (≈207 MB usable) |
| Disk | overlayfs in the Docker VM | machine rootfs **overlayfs** (no volume mounted for the bench) |
| Probe | `/proc/self/{io,stat}` + 200 ms RSS/heap/file sampler | same binary, same matrix |

Honesty notes: the local host is arm64 under Docker Desktop's linuxkit VM, so its
12 cores flatter parallel scenarios and the disk is virtualised. The Fly box is the
**single-fractional-core reality** of the cheapest deploy. Disk write-bytes are
measured via `/proc/self/io` on both; absolute disk latency is not the point here —
**relative** write amplification and the memory/file behaviour are, and those match
across platforms.

## How to reproduce

```bash
# local — builds the bench image, runs the matrix on the container's own fs
BENCH_DUR=3s ./test/bench/run-bench.sh          # → test/bench/out/results.json

# opt-in queue create/send/force-delete/converge churn
BENCH_ONLY=lifecycle_churn BENCH_DUR=2s ./test/bench/run-bench.sh

# hermetic HTTP-Hrana logical-lease trend (loopback; no Turso credentials)
go test ./engine -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkHranaSingleLeaseExec$' -benchmem -benchtime=3s
```

The historical Fly run used an environment-specific deployment file that is not
part of this repository. Reproduce cloud measurements by deploying the committed
`test/bench/Dockerfile` with your own explicit machine, region, volume and cleanup
configuration, and record those inputs with the result.

Time-driven scenarios run for `dur` (3 seconds in the historical matrix); the
fixed-volume drain and bloat scenarios instead run until their capped prefill is
accounted for. Every scenario then enters an **idle + GC + FreeOSMemory** phase so
we can measure what is *reclaimed*. A 200 ms background sampler records RSS + Go
heap + DB/WAL file sizes throughout, and each scenario prints a `[done]` or `[fail]`
line as it finishes (so a constrained box that stops early still leaves diagnostics
for the scenarios already attempted).

The runner fails closed on workload operation errors: fixed-volume drains must match
their exact prefill, mixed workloads reconcile accepted messages with completed plus
remaining messages, and result-file failures produce a nonzero exit. For remote `-db`
runs, use a dedicated non-production database. Each process uses a unique queue
namespace, force-deletes only that namespace after every scenario, and drives bounded
cleanup; an interrupted process can still leave its private namespace behind.

The opt-in `lifecycle_churn` scenario uses a fixed set of 64 queue names and never
reuses a name until deletion has converged. Each cycle creates the queues, sends
small batches, accepts forced deletion, and runs bounded maintenance until every
name is absent. Four queues carry 1,024 messages so the test covers pending cleanup;
the other 60 carry 16 messages. The live message-body payload stays below 1 MiB.
Its result reports immediate and pending acknowledgements, maintenance passes,
convergence latency, peak payload, and DB/WAL size. Here `ops/s` means fully
converged queue lifecycles per second; the generic latency columns measure the
initial delete acknowledgement.

A final 2-second native force-deletion smoke run on an Apple M1 Pro completed
640 queue lifecycles (10 cycles) at 289.17 lifecycles/s. All 640 deletions were
accepted, 40 required background-style cleanup, convergence p99/max was
67.519/85.309 ms, and the database peaked at 5.528 MiB before ending at
0.480 MiB with a zero-byte WAL. This short run
is a regression signal, not a deployment capacity claim; reproduce it on the target
CPU, filesystem, durability mode, message sizes, and remote backend when applicable.

Native Go benchmarks cover topic fan-out, subscription create/empty-delete churn,
and exact-total subscription pagination:

```bash
go test ./engine -run '^$' \
  -bench 'Benchmark(TopicFanout|SubscriptionCreateDelete|ListSubscriptionsPage)' \
  -benchmem -count=5
```

On an Apple M1 Pro with Go 1.26.9, the final recorded medians were
323.955 µs per create/delete lifecycle with 100 retained subscriptions and
328.866 µs with 10,000 retained subscriptions (1.015×). A 100-item page with
an exact total measured 0.652 ms at 1,000 subscriptions and 5.168 ms at 10,000.
A smoke with 5,000 queued messages acknowledged force deletion in 3.203 ms and
converged in one 29.367 ms maintenance pass. These control-plane measurements
found no strong lifecycle regression, but the exact count scales with inventory;
do not treat the 10,000-subscription safety ceiling as a low-latency guarantee.

The native suite also covers fixed-lifetime fan-out and indexed subscription-expiry
passes:

```bash
go test ./engine -run '^$' \
  -bench 'Benchmark(TopicFanoutTTL32|SubscriptionExpiry)' \
  -benchmem -count=5
```

On the same Apple M1 Pro with Go 1.26.9, seven alternating one-second rounds
compared the fixed-lifetime implementation with the same suite before TTL support.
Median latency changed by +2.50% for `SendOne`, -0.43% for `SendBatch64`, -3.32%
for 32-way topic fan-out, -0.45% for 256-way fan-out, and +0.86% for receive plus
complete. All remained below the 10% investigation threshold. In a separate
same-binary comparison, 32-way fixed-lifetime fan-out had a 1.512 ms median,
3.62% above permanent subscriptions by independent medians; it added 32
allocations and 255 bytes per publish. Shared-host variation means neither the
small gains nor this small cost is an optimization or SLA claim.

An indexed expiry scan over 10,000 future deadlines took 56.808 µs per no-work
pass (17,603 passes/s). Transitioning a full 1,000-subscription due batch took
3.306 ms (302,459 subscriptions/s). A controlled burst created 10,000
subscriptions with one 5,000-message backlog, then advanced them to one common
deadline. Data-plane fencing was immediate; 19 manually driven bounded passes
discarded the backlog and removed all metadata in 338 ms. With normal background
workers, 10,000 empty subscriptions converged in 1.292 s. A permanent queue had
no send errors during cleanup; its send p50 stayed near 0.1 ms, while p99 rose
from 0.687 ms before expiry to 12.003 ms during the burst (34.499 ms maximum).
This is the expected bounded tail-latency cost of many simultaneous expirations,
not a capacity promise; stagger deadlines and load-test the target backend.

Adding required lifecycle timestamps to 100-item subscription pages changed the
1,000-item inventory median from 0.658 ms to 0.712 ms (+8.21%) and the 10,000-item
median from 5.187 ms to 5.325 ms (+2.66%). Page memory fell from about 39 KB to
30 KB after exact preallocation; allocation counts stayed effectively flat.

## Observation cost under a deep current backlog

The native observation benchmarks use 300 queues with 300,000 messages retained at
the same time. This is current backlog, not cumulative broker throughput: completed
messages normally leave the table when settled. Run the committed fixtures with:

```bash
go test ./engine -run '^$' \
  -bench 'Benchmark(ObservationDeepBacklog|SendDuringDeepObservation)$' \
  -benchmem -count=3
```

Per-queue `Stats` uses state-specific indexes. Global `Observe` must still scan the
retained rows when its roughly 10-second shared cache needs a refresh; cache hits
still allocate and serialize the full queue response. The deliberately hostile
`continuous_observe` benchmark calls observation as fast as possible and is a
stress case, not a recommended scrape interval.

The final aggregate query replaced per-state `SUM` expressions with selective
`COUNT ... FILTER` aggregates while keeping one grouped scan. On an Apple M1 Pro
with Go 1.26.9, three measured refreshes in each of three runs produced:

| Current retained distribution | Earlier `SUM` median | Current `FILTER` median | Median change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 300,000 active | 248.369 ms | 210.754 ms | -15.14% |
| 50,000 in each of six states | 244.973 ms | 210.518 ms | -14.06% |

This isolates aggregate-expression cost; it is not a deployment capacity result.
The refresh remains proportional to retained rows and competes for CPU, page cache,
storage bandwidth, and WAL checkpoint headroom even though a local file uses a
separate read-only observation connection.

A five-pair local-file pressure run compared baseline and monitored 20-second
phases at 1,000 scheduled sends/s. Each monitored phase made the expected global
refreshes and per-queue calls; every admitted message completed and each phase
ended with zero backlog. The preselected paired-median 10% investigation threshold
failed for every foreground p99 measure:

| Measure | Paired-median monitored change |
|---|---:|
| Throughput | -1.06% |
| Dropped offered slots | +1.05 percentage points |
| Send p99 | +18.50% |
| Receive p99 | +14.80% |
| Complete p99 | +53.03% |
| End-to-end p99 | +154.12% |

Host variation was material and individual pairs moved in both directions, so the
run supports stable throughput and completed-work accounting at that offered load.
It does **not** show that monitoring has no foreground tail-latency cost. A separate
500 sends/s run also contained one severe adverse window, so it did not establish a
tail-latency-safe operating point.

Monitored WAL peaks were 4.32–5.34 times their paired baselines in the 1,000/s run.
After each phase, a passive checkpoint reported no busy reader and all frames
checkpointed; a following truncating checkpoint left a zero-byte WAL. Observation
can therefore cause transient WAL growth even when the file is reclaimable after
the reader finishes. Start production scraping at 15 seconds, then measure refresh
duration, WAL growth, and foreground p99 with the target backlog and hardware.

## Remote Turso trend soak

The manually dispatched **Turso performance soak** Action exercises one
package-internal Engine directly against the dedicated verification database.
It is separate from the HTTP broker and uses four closed-loop lanes: two standard
queues, one `group_fifo` queue and one `strict_fifo` queue. Each lane repeatedly
sends one unique 256-byte body, receives and verifies that exact body, then
completes it before starting the next cycle. This keeps the live message working
set bounded while exercising normal background maintenance.

The four logical lanes share a fixed admission limit of one harness database
call in flight (`foreground_max_in_flight=1` in `metadata.json`). Their initial
starts use nominal 0, 250, 500 and 750 ms offsets, recorded as a 250 ms lane-start
stagger in the metadata. Against the four-connection remote pool, this avoids a
synchronized startup burst and keeps foreground call demand below the pool limit,
providing headroom for normal background maintenance. The profile is deliberately
a sustainable stability and trend load. It is not a capacity test, and its
throughput must not be read as the backend's maximum.

The admission limit applies only to calls made by the harness. Engine background
workers bypass it, and it does not reserve the Turso primary's serialized write
lock.

Choose 2, 10 or 30 minutes when dispatching the workflow. Start with 2 minutes to
verify credentials, cleanup and evidence collection; use 30 minutes for the
intended sustained trend check. The workflow and the existing Turso nightly suite
share one repository-wide concurrency lock because both use `TestMain` to reset
the same database. Both workflows have a fail-closed allowlist for the
verification host before tests can reset it. Never point either workflow at a
production database.

Each minute, and once more for a final partial window, the artifact records
per-lane and overall cycles/s; Send, Receive, Complete and end-to-end p50/p95/p99
and maximum latency; empty/error counts; queue backlog; settlement-receipt
counts; storage outcomes and retries; pool waits; background-maintenance pass
state; Go heap, RSS, goroutines, GC and process CPU where the runner exposes them.
The maintenance snapshot is copied from process memory and does not issue an
additional remote database query. `metadata.json`, `windows.jsonl`,
`summary.json`, `summary.md` and the test log are retained for 14 days. Errors,
body mismatches, accounting failures, final backlog or exact cleanup failures
fail the run, while the evidence written before a failure remains uploadable.

A single non-final `Stats` or settlement-receipt-count sample that fails with the
`connection` category is recorded as a gap and may recover at the next scheduled
sample; the harness does not issue an extra query to force recovery. During that
gap, the overall and per-lane backlog and settlement-receipt fields are `null`,
and older values are not presented as final state. A second monitoring failure
anywhere in the run, any other operation or error category (including a
working-set invariant), or a failed final sample fails the soak. Each window
records structured monitoring status, and the summary records the failed-sample
count and recovery status.

A single failed maintenance pass may recover on that task's next complete pass.
Two consecutive failed passes, or one still unrecovered at the end of the run,
fail the soak. Recovered failures remain visible in the cumulative maintenance
counters and bounded diagnostic history. The final maintenance judgement is a
process-memory snapshot taken after `Engine.Close` has stopped and joined the
background workers; the harness does not trigger an extra maintenance pass to
change the result. Thus the last `windows.jsonl` entry is the pre-cleanup workload
sample, while `summary.json.final_maintenance` is the post-close terminal state.
A runner cancellation or outer test timeout can interrupt final cleanup; the
next run's `TestMain` reset and namespaced startup cleanup remove that residue.

The first-to-last window change is descriptive and has no performance threshold
because GitHub-hosted runner placement, shared CPU and network path add noise.
Turso does not expose physical database or WAL file sizes through this client;
those JSON fields are `null`, never a misleading zero. Settlement receipts have
30-minute retention, so a 30-minute run's final receipt count is a current
retention snapshot rather than a lifetime completion total.

## 1 · Throughput & write amplification

256 B bodies unless noted. `wB/op` = bytes physically written to disk per op (write
amplification). **The local box is 12 fast cores; the cloud box is one fraction of a
throttled core** — read the two columns as "engine character" vs "cheapest real box".

| scenario | sync | local ops/s | cloud ops/s | local wB/op | cloud wB/op |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| produce_p1 | NORMAL | 15,926 | **4,000** | 9,740 | 9,696 |
| produce_p4 | NORMAL | 17,449 | **567** | 9,744 | 9,667 |
| produce_p8 | NORMAL | 17,963 | **322** | 9,745 | 9,635 |
| batch_16_p4 | NORMAL | 30,748 | 1,600 | 1,979 | 1,928 |
| batch_64_p4 | NORMAL | 35,146 | **6,000** | 1,090 | 1,045 |
| e2e_4x4 | NORMAL | 4,413 | 197 | 58,539 | 55,809 |
| sessions_64g | NORMAL | 3,789 | 164 | 71,016 | 67,794 |
| produce_p4_FULL | **FULL** | 1,556 | 468 | 13,743 | 13,682 |
| props_p4 | NORMAL | 15,909 | 1,000 | 10,577 | 10,493 |
| props_batch64 | NORMAL | 24,161 | **6,700** | 1,641 | 1,622 |

**Write amplification was similar in these two runs** — every cloud `wB/op` is
within 5% of its local counterpart. The samples suggest that SQLite + WAL dominate
this cost (a 256 B message was about 9.7 KB written singly and 1.1 KB batched), but
two environments do not establish a platform-independent constant. Measure the
target filesystem and workload before capacity planning.

**On a single fractional core, concurrency *hurts*** — `produce_p1` 4.0k >
`produce_p4` 567 > `produce_p8` 322. With `GOMAXPROCS=1` there's no parallelism to
exploit, so more producers just add lock contention + scheduler/GC thrash on the one
writer. On the cheap box the right pattern is **one producer that batches**, not many
concurrent single-sends.

**Batching is the great equaliser** — `batch_64` does 6.0k/s on the *same* throttled
core that only manages 567/s of single `produce_p4` (≈10×), at ~1/9 the write
amplification. Enriched batched sends (`props_batch64`) hold 6.7k/s.

**FULL durability** costs ~11× locally; on the already-CPU-bound cloud box the gap
narrows (468 vs 567) because fsync isn't the bottleneck there — the core is.

## 2 · Memory footprint after a short idle

Whole-process **RSS** (not just Go heap), peak during load vs after the harness's
short 1.9-second idle and forced GC. This end snapshot describes immediate process
state; it does not imply that the 60-second storage janitor has run.

| scenario | local peak → short idle | cloud peak → short idle |
|---|---:|---:|
| produce_p8 | 34 → 27 MB | 27 → 20 MB |
| batch_64_p4 | 32 → 27 MB | 28 → 23 MB |
| props_batch64 | 33 → 29 MB | 29 → 25 MB |
| size_16KB | 33 → 29 MB | 27 → 23 MB |
| drain_4c (200k msgs) | 33 → 28 MB | — (see §7) |

**Peak RSS was 27–34 MB across the scenarios listed above.** The local 200k-message
drain and 16 KB body scenarios stayed within that measured range. SQLite stores
the backlog on disk, but this does not bound all broker memory. RSS declined after
load stopped; no sustained growth was observed in these runs. Larger messages,
more concurrent requests or queues, and monitoring can change the footprint.
Measure the current workload before choosing a memory limit.

## 3 · DB-file footprint and reclamation

`bloat_50k` now inserts exactly 50,000 messages once, samples the full backlog,
drains exactly that count with `Complete`, and rejects any send, receive, settle,
or accounting error. `file_bytes_per_msg` uses the count actually accepted during
prefill. Older results from this scenario are not comparable: the previous harness
prefilled twice, rounded each tail batch up, and still divided file size by 50,000.

The scenario's `db_final_mb` is the immediate state after the same 1.9-second idle
used by the other scenarios. It is useful for comparing the peak with the drained
file, but it does not verify background page reclamation. Local file databases use
`auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL`; the background janitor checks every 60 seconds and
reclaims a bounded number of pages once its freelist threshold is met. Use a run
that spans that interval, or measure an explicit `Compact(false)`, when evaluating
reclamation. Remote Turso manages its own storage.

## 4 · Enriched messages — KV properties

`props_*` send a realistic message: a `Properties` map (tenant / trace_id /
event_type / priority / source / schema_ver) plus CorrelationID, Subject,
ContentType — "normal usage", vs a bare body.

| scenario | local ops/s | fileB/msg | vs bare |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| produce_p4 (bare) | 17,449 | 415 | — |
| props_p4 | 15,909 | 693 | +280 B/msg on disk, ~9 % slower |
| batch_64_p4 (bare) | 35,146 | 373 | — |
| props_batch64 | 24,161 | 664 | +291 B/msg, ~31 % slower batched |

Properties are cheap on a single send (~9 % throughput, +280 B/msg) but cost more when
batched (~31 %): once commit overhead is amortised away, the per-message JSON-encode of
the KV map becomes the dominant work.

## 5 · Body-size sweep

4 producers, NORMAL, body 64 B → 16 KB:

| body | local ops/s | cloud ops/s | wB/op (≈both) | fileB/msg |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 B | 17,205 | 1,200 | 9,122 | 217 |
| 256 B | 17,449 | 567 | 9,744 | 415 |
| 1 KB | 13,991 | 912 | 12,980 | 1,489 |
| 4 KB | 12,547 | 454 | 22,205 | 4,740 |
| 16 KB | 7,988 | 259 | 46,939 | 17,091 |

On-disk storage was roughly linear with body size in this sweep. The measured
difference between body size and `fileB/msg` ranged from 153 to 707 bytes, so the
table does not support one fixed row/index-overhead constant. Throughput was
commit-bound up to about 256 B and then increasingly byte-bound. Default body cap
is 1 MiB (`MaxMessageBytes`).

## 6 · Load ramp & consumer churn (local)

- **rampdown_4x4**: produce hard, then stop producing while consumers drain to idle.
  RSS peak 31 MB → 27 MB after the load goes away — memory tracks the workload *down*,
  not a one-way ratchet.
- **churn_consumers**: producers steady while consumer cohorts repeatedly go
  **online/offline**. RSS stays ~28–34 MB across cycles with **no stair-step growth** —
  connect/disconnect doesn't leak.

## 7 · Cloud reality — what a 256 MB fractional core changes

The Fly `shared-cpu-1x` is `GOMAXPROCS=1` with CPU-steal. Versus the 12-core local box:

1. **Memory stayed low in the measured scenarios.** Peak RSS was 27–29 MB for
   the cloud scenarios in §2, with reclamation after load. This does not establish
   the memory required by other workloads or current releases.
2. **Write amplification was close in these two runs.** Cloud values were within
   5% of local; validate that relationship on the target storage stack.
3. **Throughput: core-bound, and concurrency backfires.** Single-send multi-producer
   collapses (567/s at p4, 322/s at p8) because there's no second core. **Batch, and
   throughput recovers to thousands/s** (6.0–6.7k).
4. **Tail latency: throttling shows up.** p99 hits the 100 ms histogram ceiling on most
   multi-goroutine scenarios (CPU-steal stalls); single-producer scenarios keep p99
   under ~5 ms.

In this short historical sample, batching reached about 6k msg/s on a
shared-cpu-1x, while concurrent single sends reached only hundreds/s. These are
workload observations, not a sustained-capacity or SLA claim.

## Tuning knobs

mqlite ships sensible defaults; most deployments change nothing. In rough order of impact:

| knob | default | when to change |
|---|---|---|
| **batch size** (`messages:[…]`) | — | the biggest lever — ~9× less write amplification, ~2× throughput. Batch whenever you can. |
| **`MQLITE_SYNC`** | `NORMAL` | `FULL` only if a power cut losing the last few commits is unacceptable; it costs ~11–18× on single sends, so pair it with batching. |
| `wal_autocheckpoint` | 1000 pages (~4 MB) | matched the no-long-reader historical baseline; observation snapshots and other readers can cause a larger transient WAL. Raise only after measuring the checkpoint and recovery trade-off. |
| `cache_size` | ~2 MB | the working set (queue heads + indexes) is small; raise only after profiling shows cache pressure under deep backlogs — it costs RAM on a 256 MB machine. |
| `mmap_size` | off | `modernc.org/sqlite` is pure-Go; don't assume C-SQLite mmap gains — measure first. |
| writer/provider pool | local writer 1 / remote provider 4 | **don't change** — the local writer pool stays at one for atomic claims; local files also have one read-only observation connection. The remote pool is scoped to one broker and Turso serializes commits. `libsql://` logical connections are single-lease while the shared HTTP transport retains TCP/TLS reuse; see [turso.md](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/turso.md). |

`busy_timeout=5000` and `temp_store=MEMORY` are set on local modernc SQLite
connections. They do not apply to remote Turso/libSQL connections, whose transient
contention uses the bounded retry policy described in [turso.md](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/turso.md).

## Findings summary

1. **Low measured memory with reclamation** — peak RSS was 27–34 MB in the
   scenarios in §2. No sustained growth was observed during the recorded churn
   and ramp-down tests; validate the current workload separately.
2. **Batch to go fast** — ~9× less write amplification, and on a single core the
   difference between *hundreds/s* and *thousands/s*.
3. **Write amplification was similar in two historical environments** (~9.7 KB/op
   single, ~1.1 KB batched, with local/cloud pairs within 5%); it is not a universal
   platform constant.
4. **Single-writer model**: more producers ≠ more write throughput; on one core they
   make it *worse*. Prefer one batching producer.
5. **Peak backlog is a primary sizing input.** Add headroom for WAL, page/index
   overhead, fragmentation, reclamation lag, long readers and backups; background
   `incremental_vacuum` returns eligible free pages over time.
6. **NORMAL vs FULL** is an ~11× durability dial (local); pick per host failure model.
7. **Properties are affordable**; large bodies are byte-bound and storage-linear.

The historical source artifacts were captured in `test/bench/out/results.json`
and the `mqlite-bench` Fly logs; they are not shipped in this repository. Treat
the table as historical evidence and rerun the commands above before using the
numbers for a current deployment decision.


<!-- ===== mqlite main · source v0.4.1; latest supported release v0.4.0 · docs/conformance.md ===== -->

# Conformance — correct mqlite behavior (TCK)

This is the normative spec of how mqlite **must** behave — the invariants that define
"correct," independent of any one implementation detail. Each is enforced by a
hermetic test (cross-referenced); together these are mqlite's TCK. If a change would
break a **MUST** here, it is a behavior change, not a refactor.

Default Peek-Lock delivery is **at-least-once**: redelivery is possible, so
handlers must be idempotent. Receive-and-delete is the caller's explicit
at-most-once broker-removal path and removes a message before returning it; the
same receive attempt ID can replay its saved response. Other documented
discard paths include message TTL configured to discard, DLQ retention, forced
resource deletion, and fixed subscription expiry. (§1.7, §3, §8, §14)

## 1 · Peek-Lock lifecycle

- **1.1** `Receive` claims an `active` message, moving it to `locked` for the queue's
  lock duration, and returns a `lock_token`. *(engine/functional_test.go)*
- **1.2** A `locked` message MUST be invisible to other `Receive` calls until it is
  settled or its lock expires — no message is delivered to two consumers at once.
  *(engine/functional_test.go `TestCompetingConsumersNoDouble`)*
- **1.3** Each newly granted `Receive` or `ReceiveDeferred` claim increments
  `delivery_count` exactly once. Renewal, settlement, lock reaping, scheduled
  activation and replay of a live receive attempt MUST NOT increment it.
  *(engine/engine_test.go, engine/ga_fixes_test.go, engine/functional_test.go)*
- **1.4** When a lock expires, the reaper returns the message to `active` (redelivery)
  — or to `dead_lettered` once `delivery_count >= max_delivery_count`. *(engine/engine_test.go)*
- **1.5** Claims are O(log n) on a deep backlog (a partial index on `active` rows; the
  reaper, not the claim path, reclaims expired locks). *(engine/claim_plan_test.go)*
- **1.6 Claim time.** `Receive` (with or without an `AttemptID`, including receive-and-delete)
  and `ReceiveDeferred` MUST evaluate TTL eligibility and lease deadlines using fresh broker time
  after writer admission, for each claimed item and each remote retry. A message whose TTL has
  expired at that check MUST NOT be claimed. Waiting for the writer or processing an earlier batch
  item MUST NOT consume a later item's lease before its claim begins.
  *(engine/functional_test.go: TestClaimTimeAfterWriterAdmission, TestClaimBatchUsesEachItemsTime,
  TestClaimBatchTTLBetweenItems, TestReceiveDeferredMixedItemsAndCommittedPrefix;
  engine/storage_test.go: TestClaimTimeRefreshesOnRemoteRetry)*

- **1.7 Receive-and-delete** removes each returned row and grants no lease: its
  lock token is empty and deadline is zero, including a cached attempt replay.
  Peek-lock retains its token and lease deadline. *(sdk_test.go: TestSDKReceiveDeleteLeaseShape)*

## 2 · Settlement (fenced on `lock_token`)

Exactly one verb per outcome; new effects require the `lock_token` from `Receive`
and an unexpired lease, with the exact-request replay exception in §2.6.

- **2.1 Complete** removes the message. *(engine/functional_test.go)*
- **2.2 Abandon** returns it to `active` for redelivery (or `dead_lettered` at/above
  max). With `delay_ms > 0` it parks in `scheduled` until the backoff lapses
  (scheduler re-activates it); on an **ordered** queue the parked head holds
  head-of-line exactly like a scheduled send — successors cannot overtake it
  (§5.5). Neither Abandon nor scheduled activation increments `delivery_count`;
  the next claim does. *(engine/engine_test.go; engine/functional_test.go:
  TestAbandonDelayHoldsGroupOrder)*
- **2.3 Reject** moves it to `dead_lettered` with a reason. *(engine/functional_test.go)*
- **2.4 Defer** sets it aside; it is retrieved later by seq via `ReceiveDeferred`.
  Normal `Receive` never returns a deferred message. In an **ordered** queue a deferred
  message **holds the head-of-line** — later messages in its group (or the whole queue
  under `strict_fifo`) are not claimable until it is retrieved and settled; other groups
  proceed. There is no automatic recovery without a TTL (the reaper never reclaims
  deferred rows); recover a lost seq via `Peek state=deferred`. A successful
  `ReceiveDeferred` increments `delivery_count` but does not gate that explicit
  by-sequence claim on `max_delivery_count`; it can therefore return a count above
  the ordinary delivery budget. Subsequent settlement follows the usual rules.
  *(engine/functional_test.go: TestDeferHoldsHeadOfLine)*
- **2.5 Renew** MUST preserve the same state, token, and `delivery_count`. For a
  queue or subscription without a fixed expiry it sets the deadline to
  `max(old locked_until, broker now + lock_duration)`; a fixed subscription
  lifetime caps the candidate deadline. It MUST NOT shorten a lease or revive one
  whose current deadline has passed. *(engine/ga_fixes_test.go)*
- **2.6** Settling with a wrong/expired token MUST fail with `ErrLockLost` (HTTP 409)
  — **except** an idempotent replay with a live receipt for the exact request (§3.2) returns
  success. Matching the token alone is insufficient: new settlement and renewal effects
  require a locked row with `locked_until_ms > now`, including before the reaper runs.
  The equality boundary is expired. Time is sampled after local writer admission and
  afresh for each settlement statement and remote retry; waiting cannot preserve an
  expired lease or receipt. A live exact-request receipt can still replay a previously
  committed effect after the original lease expires.
  *(engine/ga_fixes_test.go; engine/complete_batch_test.go:
  TestSettlementLeaseDeadline, TestSettlementReceiptIdentityMatrix,
  TestSettlementReceiptTimeAfterWriterAdmission, TestCompleteBatchRefreshesTimeBetweenChunks;
  engine/storage_test.go: TestSettlementTimeRefreshesOnRemoteRetry;
  sdk_test.go: TestSDKSettlementDeadline)*
- **2.7 CompleteBatch** settles many messages in one transaction with the same per-item
  fencing + idempotency; a stale token without an exact-request receipt yields `ok=false`,
  never failing the batch. Single `Complete` and a `CompleteBatch` item share the completed
  operation identity, so the same successful request can replay in either direction.
  *(engine/complete_batch_test.go: TestCompleteBatch, TestSettlementReceiptIdentityMatrix)*
- **2.8 RenewBatch** extends a whole batch's leases in ONE statement, fenced per item on its own
  `lock_token`, and reports the deadline it committed. `ok=true` means the lease was live when the
  broker's STATEMENT finished — the answer still has to travel, so `locked_until_ms` is the
  authoritative fact and the caller compares it against its own clock. A renewal whose write
  outlived the lock reports `ok=false` rather than handing back a lock the caller never held, and a
  renewal never *shortens* a lease. Each successful item uses the same deadline rule
  as §2.5 and preserves state, token, and `delivery_count`. Capped at 512 messages —
  a claim about a live lease is only keepable within a single statement.
  *(engine/complete_batch_test.go)*

## 3 · Idempotency & at-least-once

- **3.1** On `Open`, every orphaned `locked` row (a crash leftover) MUST be
  reclaimed under the same rule as the reaper: back to `active`, or to
  `dead_lettered` (`MaxDeliveryCountExceeded`) once `delivery_count >=
  max_delivery_count` — a crash never buys an extra delivery.
  *(engine/engine_test.go: TestCrashRecoveryRespectsMaxDelivery)*
- **3.2** While its exact-request receipt is live, a settle whose response was lost MUST
  replay as success, not `ErrLockLost` — and ONLY when it is the same request.
  A `settlement_receipt` identifies
  `queue + seq_number + lock_token + operation + effect-bearing arguments`; a call that
  differs in ANY of them is not a replay and MUST return `ErrLockLost`, never a success
  that silently keeps the first call's effect.
  *(engine/ga_fixes_test.go; engine/complete_batch_test.go: TestReceiptsAreBoundToTheirMessage,
  TestReceiptsAreBoundToTheirArguments, TestSettlementReceiptsAreVerbSpecific,
  TestSettlementReceiptIdentityMatrix;
  engine/model_test.go: TestEngineMatchesTheModel, TestModelRejectReceiptArguments)*
- **3.3** A `Receive` retried with the same `AttemptID` MUST replay the same batch /
  same lock tokens while its attempt record is live. Record expiry MUST be checked against
  fresh time after writer admission; a record that expires during the wait MUST NOT replay.
  *(engine/ga_fixes_test.go; engine/functional_test.go: TestReceiveAttemptExpiryAfterWriterWait)*
- **3.4** No message loss + no content corruption: a contiguous `1..N` sequence with
  random bodies (hashed into a property), consumed concurrently with redelivery, is
  delivered completely (every value once) and intact (each body matches its hash).
  *(engine/integrity_test.go `TestMessageIntegrity`)*

## 4 · Deduplication

- **4.1** Within a queue's `dedup_window`, a repeat `message_id` (empty → body SHA-256)
  MUST collapse to a single enqueue. *(engine/functional_test.go, engine/turso_test.go)*
- **4.2** A *single* `Send` whose `message_id` conflicts with a different body MUST
  return `ErrDedupConflict` (HTTP 409). *(server/send_dedup_test.go)*
- **4.3** In a *multi-message* `Send`, a conflicting slot comes back as seq `0`
  (skipped) while the rest of the batch commits. *(wire `SendResponse`; server/send_dedup_test.go)*

## 5 · Ordering modes

- **5.1 `standard`** — per-`GroupID` FIFO with cross-group parallelism; messages with no
  `GroupID` are unordered. Claim eligibility is identical to `group_fifo` — the only
  difference is `group_fifo` additionally requires a `GroupID` at send time. *(engine/functional_test.go)*
- **5.2 `group_fifo`** — strict FIFO per `GroupID` (head-of-line per group); a send
  without a `GroupID` MUST be rejected with `ErrGroupRequired`. *(engine/functional_test.go)*
- **5.3 `strict_fifo`** — global FIFO: at most one message in flight for the queue at a
  time. *(engine/functional_test.go, engine/claim_plan_test.go)*
- **5.4** Head-of-line MUST survive lock expiry: an expired-but-not-yet-reaped lock
  still blocks its group (`strict_fifo`: the whole queue) — successors are never
  delivered ahead of the expired head, and once the reaper resettles it the head is
  redelivered first, in id order (or dead-lettered at `count ≥ max`, which unblocks
  the group). The accepted cost is a group stall of up to one reaper interval on a
  consumer timeout. *(engine/functional_test.go: TestFIFOHoldsAcrossLockExpiry)*
- **5.5** Head-of-line MUST survive an explicit backoff: `Abandon` with `delay_ms > 0`
  parks the head in `scheduled` — a state the head-of-line probe covers — so
  successors are never delivered ahead of a backing-off head; when the backoff lapses
  the scheduler re-activates it and it is redelivered first. Other groups (other
  queues' worth of work under `standard`/`group_fifo`) proceed during the backoff.
  *(engine/functional_test.go: TestAbandonDelayHoldsGroupOrder)*

## 6 · Dead-letter queue

- **6.1** Reaching `max_delivery_count` on an ordinary Peek-Lock `Receive` MUST NOT itself
  dead-letter the message: the Nth ordinary Peek-Lock claim is a full final attempt and may
  be renewed and completed. If that locked attempt is Abandoned, its lease expires,
  or it is recovered at startup with `delivery_count >= max_delivery_count`, it MUST be
  dead-lettered with reason `MaxDeliveryCountExceeded` instead of becoming active
  for an ordinary Peek-Lock N+1 claim. This ordinary retry bound does not override the
  explicit `ReceiveDeferred` behavior in §2.4. *(engine/engine_test.go)*
- **6.2** `Redrive` moves dead letters back to `active` (or to a target queue); `Purge`
  permanently deletes them (scoped by `Max`/`OlderThanMs`). *(engine/redrive — functional tests)*

## 7 · Scheduling, deferral & TTL

- **7.1 Schedule** keeps a message hidden (`scheduled`, `visible_at` in the future)
  until its time, then the scheduler activates it; `Cancel` deletes a scheduled
  message that has never been delivered (`delivery_count=0`) — a backoff-parked
  redelivery (§2.2) is NOT cancellable and stays under the retry/DLQ discipline.
  Scheduler activation MUST NOT increment `delivery_count`.
  *(engine/functional_test.go: TestAbandonDelayHoldsGroupOrder)*
- **7.2 TTL** — an expired message (`expires_at`) MUST move to the DLQ when the queue
  has `dead_letter_on_expire`, else be discarded. The two branches cover the **same
  state set** — every non-terminal state including `scheduled`. The TTL sweep can
  expire a scheduled row directly. If the scheduler observes an overdue row first,
  it may change that row to `active`, but claim eligibility still excludes it at
  `now >= expires_at`; the TTL sweep then terminates it without delivery. The queue
  default is both the default and ceiling for an explicit message TTL. Expiry is
  anchored at the message's initial `visible_at`, so for scheduled messages the
  clock starts at their delivery time; later delayed Abandon and scheduler
  activation MUST NOT recompute it. Message TTL is independent of the lock lease:
  it may expire a locked row, and Renew MUST NOT extend it. Embedded and remote
  batch Send MUST preserve each item's requested TTL; a uniform HTTP batch may use
  the batch-wide field, while a mixed batch uses per-message fields. A request that
  combines a positive batch-wide TTL with positive per-message TTLs, or supplies a
  negative TTL in either location, MUST fail as invalid. The Go SDK MUST also reject
  a positive message TTL below the wire's 1 ms precision before sending or writing,
  and an effective deadline that overflows epoch milliseconds MUST fail without
  committing any item in the batch.
  *(engine/functional_test.go: TestTTLScheduledToDeadLetter,
  TestTTLCapAtQueueDefault, TestNegativeMessageTTLRejectedBeforeWrite,
  TestMessageTTLExpiryOverflowRejectedAtomically,
  TestMessageTTLDeadlineSurvivesRenewAndDelayedRetry; sdk_test.go:
  TestBatchTTLRemoteEmbeddedParity, TestNegativeMessageTTLSDKParity,
  TestRemoteBatchTTLWireCompatibility; server/send_dedup_test.go:
  TestServerSendPerMessageTTL; engine/turso_test.go:
  TestTursoMessageTTLParity; test/api_tests.py: t_message_ttl_contract)*

## 8 · DLQ retention

- **8.1** With a bound set, `reapDLQ` MUST drop **oldest-first** dead letters past the
  max age, per-queue count, or per-queue body bytes — and MUST touch **only**
  `state='dead_lettered'` (never undelivered/in-flight/scheduled work). These are
  asynchronous retention targets rather than admission limits; a DLQ MAY exceed
  them temporarily between bounded worker passes.
  *(engine/retention_dlq_test.go)*
- **8.2** With no bound (the engine default), the DLQ is unbounded — no auto-deletion.
  *(engine/retention_dlq_test.go `TestDLQRetentionDisabledByDefault`)*
- **8.3** Each queue's effective bound is its own override resolved against the engine
  default (`effectiveBound`): `0` inherits the default, `>0` overrides it, `<0` is
  explicitly unbounded. *(engine/retention_dlq_test.go `TestEffectiveBound`,
  `TestDLQRetentionPerQueueOverride`, `TestDLQRetentionPerQueueInheritAndOptOut`)*

## 9 · Auth & errors (broker)

- **9.1** When `MQLITE_TOKENS` is set, every endpoint MUST require a valid
  `Authorization: Bearer` token **except** the open `/` (discovery), `/healthz`, and
  the static admin console under `/ui` (when enabled — its own API calls still carry a
  token); a missing/invalid/expired/revoked token → 401 `unauthenticated`.
  *(server/errors_test.go, server/index_test.go, server/console_test.go)*
- **9.2** Errors use a JSON envelope `{code,message}` with the documented HTTP status:
  400 `invalid_argument`/`group_required` · 401 `unauthenticated` · 403
  `permission_denied` · 404 `not_found` · 409
  `already_exists`/`lock_lost`/`name_conflict`/`key_conflict`/
  `queue_not_empty`/`subscription_not_empty` · 413 `message_too_large` ·
  429 `resource_exhausted` · 500 `internal` · 503 `outcome_unknown`.
  *(server/errors_test.go; see [api-reference.md](https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite/blob/main/docs/api-reference.md))*
- **9.3** Every registered RPC MUST bind a permission in the route registration.
  Send/Schedule/Cancel require send; all other QueueService methods require listen;
  AdminService and AuthService require manage, except Observe and the opt-in
  `/metrics` endpoint also accept configured read-only monitor credentials. Metrics
  MUST be disabled by default, return 404 while disabled, and appear as `/metrics`
  in discovery only while enabled. Enabling metrics MUST require administrator
  auth. Manage includes both data permissions. Configured and managed
  administrators MUST have identical operation rights, including issuing manage
  keys. Insufficient permission MUST
  fail before the handler can read or change protected data.
  *(server/errors_test.go: TestAccessKeyCompletePermissionMatrix;
  server/metrics_test.go: TestMetricsDefaultOffAndAnonymousObserveDenied,
  TestMetricsEnabledRequiresAdministratorAuthentication, TestMetricsPermissionMatrix,
  TestMetricsDisabledSkipsDatabaseAuthentication)*
- Configured monitor credentials MUST NOT grant message access or administration,
  MUST be distinct from administrators, and MUST remain usable for fault telemetry
  without database-backed authentication. Failed collection MUST omit queue gauges
  and explicitly report unavailable data, preserving real in-memory counters.
  *(server/metrics_test.go: TestMonitorConfigurationFailsClosed,
  TestObserveStorageFailureAvailability, TestObserveAuthOutcomesAndWholeRequestCoverage)*
- **9.4** Managed keys MUST survive restart and store only a SHA-256 digest of
  their token. New tokens MUST be `mqk_` plus 64 lowercase hex characters from
  a secure random source. Existing configured tokens remain accepted exactly.
  Only the successful creation response returns a secret; list, errors and logs
  MUST NOT return tokens or digests. A duplicate public ID MUST NOT mint a second
  credential. Auth-off mode MUST refuse key management.
  *(engine/storage_test.go: TestAccessKeyLifecycle, TestAccessKeyValidation;
  server/errors_test.go: TestAccessKeyManagementLifecycleAndSecrecy,
  TestAccessKeyErrorsDoNotEchoSecrets; token_test.go)*
- **9.5** Successful revocation MUST reject subsequent authentication; already
  authorized requests may finish. Static configuration takes precedence over a
  matching database record. The SDK MUST treat permission denial as permanent in
  receive, settlement and renewal paths, without unauthorized batch fallback.
  *(server/errors_test.go: TestAccessKeyRevocationAndExpiryBoundaries;
  sdk_test.go: TestManagedKeySDKAuthorization; receiver_internal_test.go;
  cmd/mqlite/safety_test.go)*
- **9.6** Access-key lists MUST retain ID-ascending order by default. Explicit
  `created_desc` MUST order the complete result by creation time descending, then
  ID descending, with stable cursor pagination. Revocation MUST NOT move a key;
  insertion ahead of a cursor MUST NOT repeat or skip existing keys on later
  pages. Unknown sort values and unknown creation-order cursors MUST fail with
  `invalid_argument`. SDKs and tools MUST reject incorrectly ordered responses.
  *(engine/storage_test.go: TestAccessKeyCreationOrderPagination,
  TestAccessKeySortValidationAndIndex; server/errors_test.go:
  TestAccessKeyCreationOrderHTTP; wire/wire_test.go:
  TestAccessKeyCreationOrderResponseValidation; test/api_tests.py)*

## 10 · Storage & schema invariants

- **10.1** Local file / `:memory:` use a single writer (`SetMaxOpenConns(1)`); a second
  process / second `OpenEmbedded` on the same file MUST fail fast with `ErrDBLocked`.
  A local file MAY use one separate `mode=ro` plus `query_only` WAL connection
  for observation reads; it MUST reject writes and checkpoints and share the
  engine close gate. The global queue snapshot MAY be reused for about 10
  seconds, MUST preserve its original
  `sampled_at_ms` and internal topology fence as one cache entry, MUST coalesce
  concurrent refreshes, and MUST NOT cache a failed refresh. Observe
  `server_time_ms` MUST be read separately from the same injectable lifecycle
  clock and MUST NOT be retained in that queue snapshot cache. Per-queue `Stats`
  remains a fresh indexed read.
  *(engine/storage_test.go, engine/observability_performance_test.go)*
- **10.2** `Open` MUST refuse a DB whose recorded `schemaVersion` differs from the
  binary's (`ErrSchemaVersionMismatch`) rather than running mismatched DDL against it.
  *(engine/storage_test.go)*
- **10.3** All times are epoch-ms (UTC); the clock is injectable for deterministic
  tests. The remote (Turso) path retries transient errors with backoff; the local
  path never retries. A successful null-baton `libsql://` response closes that
  logical Hrana stream: it MUST NOT be retained in an idle slot or handed directly
  to a waiting caller. One transaction MUST remain on one logical stream through
  commit or rollback, and the local pool MUST remain MaxOpen=1 with no connection
  lifetime recycling. *(engine/storage_test.go:
  TestHranaClosedStreamIsDiscardedBeforeFreshReuse,
  TestHranaTransactionKeepsOneLease,
  TestMemoryDBSurvivesRepeatedFreshStatements; engine/turso_test.go)*
- **10.4** Access-key table and index additions remain independently additive
  inside the canonical schema. Verify complete backup/restore content,
  including active, expired and revoked credentials.
  An incompatible existing object named `access_keys` or
  `idx_access_keys_created` MUST fail rather than be overwritten or silently trusted.
  *(engine/storage_test.go: TestAccessKeySchemaAdditiveCompatibility,
  TestAccessKeySchemaConflict, TestAccessKeyCreationIndexUpgradeAndConflicts;
  test/production/restore/run.py, compat.py)*
- **10.5** Durable resource lifecycle and fixed subscription-expiry columns and
  indexes make the v0.4.0 schema token 7 incompatible with the older schema-5
  layout and intermediate schema-6 layout. Each binary MUST refuse the other's
  database rather than adding columns, restamping the token or partially opening
  it. Operators must create a fresh database and preserve the matching old
  binary/backup pair. *(engine/storage_test.go:
  TestSchemaVersionGuard, TestSchemaContentPinnedToVersionToken)*
- **10.6 Backend parity.** Given the same committed state, broker time and request,
  local SQLite and remote Turso/libSQL MUST produce the same successful result,
  validation outcome, state transition and logical sentinel error. Latency,
  temporary availability, remote transport failures (including
  `ErrOutcomeUnknown`), remote transaction-callback replay and explicitly
  operational deployment, maintenance and observation behavior MAY differ; they
  MUST NOT silently change deterministic queue semantics.
  *(engine/turso_test.go: TestTursoIntegration, TestTursoExtended,
  TestTursoMessageTTLParity, TestTursoConcurrent, TestTursoBatchSettle;
  engine/storage_test.go; server/errors_test.go; sdk_test.go)*

## 11 · Subscription filters

- **11.1** A subscription filter is one `expr` boolean predicate over the message; an
  empty filter matches every message. It is compiled + type-checked at `Subscribe`,
  and a malformed / unknown-field / non-boolean expression MUST be rejected with
  `ErrInvalidFilter` (HTTP 400 `invalid_argument`) and **not** stored — no backing
  queue is created. *(engine/filter_test.go, server/errors_test.go)*
- **11.2** The filter is evaluated at **publish** against the message env (core fields,
  `enqueued_at`/`visible_at`, the derived `subject_parts`/`body_size`/`property_keys`,
  and the body fields `body_text`/`body_json` — projected only when referenced, with
  `body_json` decoded only for a JSON content type, else `{}`); a message is routed to
  a subscription if and only if its filter returns true.
  `enqueued_at` is the publish time and `visible_at` is the delivery time (equal for an
  immediate send, the scheduled time for a delayed one), so a delay is
  `visible_at - enqueued_at`. *(engine/filter_test.go `TestFilterFanoutConditions`,
  `TestFilterScheduledMessageDelay`)*
- **11.3** Evaluation is **fail-closed**: a filter that errors or panics at runtime MUST
  leave the message unrouted to that subscription (logged) — never crashing the broker
  and never matching by default. *(engine/filter_test.go `TestEvalFilterFailClosed`)*
- **11.4** Publishing to a topic that **no** subscription filter accepts is a valid
  no-op (`SendOne`/`Schedule` return `0, nil`), not an `ErrDedupConflict`.
  *(engine/filter_test.go `TestFilterReSubscribeRecompiles`)*

## 12 · Topics & naming

- **12.1** Plain-queue names, subscription names (their backing queues) and topic
  names are **one disjoint namespace**. Every collision MUST be rejected with
  `ErrNameConflict` (HTTP 409) at creation time, in both directions: `Subscribe`
  rejects a topic naming any existing queues row (plain or backing), a subscription
  name that is a plain queue / another topic's subscription / a live topic, and
  `topic == name`; `CreateQueue` rejects a name that is live as a topic and any
  cross-kind upsert. Same-kind upserts (queue reconfig, `(topic,name)` re-subscribe)
  stay open. A failed creation MUST leave nothing behind (guards + inserts are one
  transaction).
  *(engine/functional_test.go: TestTopicQueueNamespaceDisjoint,
  TestTopicSubscriptionIsolation)*
- **12.2** Because names are disjoint, send/publish resolution is **unambiguous**:
  an active plain-queue or backing-queue name addresses that queue; an implicit
  topic name addresses its active subscription rows; any other name returns
  `ErrQueueNotFound`. Behavior after directly altering internal tables to create a
  queue/topic collision is outside the public contract.
  *(engine/functional_test.go: TestTopicQueueNamespaceDisjoint)*
- **12.3 Subscription lifecycle.** Deletion MUST select the exact `(topic,name)`
  pair. By default it MUST reject every retained message state with
  `ErrSubscriptionNotEmpty`; force is durable authorization to discard all states.
  Acceptance MUST atomically exclude the backing queue from fan-out and the data
  plane and start bounded cleanup. If that cleanup finishes in the accepting
  transaction, it MUST remove the queue and mapping and return `deleted`. Otherwise
  it MUST commit a `deleting` marker that preserves the mapping and name until a
  later transaction removes both. Restart MUST resume accepted pending cleanup
  without another force authorization. The last active subscription's retirement
  makes its implicit topic unavailable immediately.
- **12.4 Bounded inventory.** The compatibility `ListSubscriptions` operation MUST
  return every active subscription in `(topic,name)` order. The paged operation
  MUST use the same order, default to 100, reject limits above 1,000, return an
  exact total for the request's scope and optionally include deleting entries.
  Every paged row MUST carry required non-negative `created_at_ms` and
  `expires_at_ms`; zero expiry means permanent and a positive expiry MUST be
  greater than creation. An expired retained row is logically deleting.
  Its opaque cursor MUST be bound to the topic and include-deleting scope. One
  request is a consistent snapshot; pages issued as separate requests do not
  promise a frozen snapshot under concurrent changes.
- **12.5 Capacity.** The engine MUST bound active plus deleting subscriptions
  (default 10,000). Creating a new mapping at the bound returns
  `ErrSubscriptionLimit` (HTTP 429 `resource_exhausted`); re-subscribing an active
  exact pair may update its filter. A deleting entry MUST retain its slot until
  final physical cleanup. Public `CreateQueue(kind=subscription)` MUST NOT create
  a backing queue without a subscription mapping.
- **12.6 Fixed subscription lifetime.** A positive creation TTL MUST store one
  absolute deadline from the first successful transaction. Omitted/zero TTL on a
  new subscription makes it permanent; on an existing subscription it preserves
  the original lifetime. The same positive TTL is idempotent, while a different
  positive TTL MUST return `ErrNameConflict` before changing the filter. Retry,
  filter update, message activity and restart MUST NOT extend the deadline. At
  `now >= expires_at` fan-out and every direct data-plane effect MUST reject the
  subscription, cached metadata included. Locks and long polls MUST end no later
  than the deadline; Renew MUST NOT extend it, and idempotency records MUST NOT
  authorize work after it.
  *(engine/functional_test.go, engine/engine_test.go,
  engine/complete_batch_test.go; sdk_test.go; server/subscriptions_test.go)*
- **12.7 Expiry cleanup.** Expiry is durable advance authorization to discard all
  retained message states. The indexed scanner MUST transition due subscriptions
  to the existing restart-safe deletion lifecycle, while correctness remains
  independent of scan timing. Empty subscriptions MAY use set-based cleanup only
  when mapping and backing rows are removed in one transaction with exact row
  counts, including when foreign keys are off. Nonempty subscriptions remain
  subject to the global row/byte/fairness bounds, and every retained row keeps its
  capacity slot until physical removal. *(engine/lifecycle_test.go,
  engine/storage_test.go)*

## 13 · Cancellation (context deadlines)

Cancelling a call is not a way to *undo* it, and on a local store it is not a latency knob
either. The rules below are the whole contract; they are stated here, and not only in the
changelog, because a caller can observe every one of them.

- **13.1** A mqlite operation whose context is already cancelled MUST NOT execute anything. This holds
  at both boundaries — before the wait for the writer, and again after the connection is in
  hand — and before entering a local `Tx` callback.
  *(engine/cancel_test.go: TestPreCancelledNeverExecutes,
  TestCancelInTheHandoffWindowStartsNothing, TestNothingBeginsInTheLastWindowBeforeAStatement;
  sdk_test.go: TestEmbeddedTxCancellation)*
- **13.2** A caller waiting for the single writer keeps its own deadline: cancelling while
  queued MUST return promptly and MUST mutate nothing.
  *(engine/cancel_test.go: TestCancelWhileWaitingWritesNothing)*
- **13.3** On a **local** store (file or `:memory:`), a statement that has already begun
  executing MUST be allowed to finish. It is not interrupted, and **there is no upper bound on
  how long it takes** — `EngineTx.SQL()` runs arbitrary user SQL, a full `VACUUM` rewrites the
  file, a large `Purge` is a big `DELETE`. A write can therefore commit *after* its caller has
